knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a Power of a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express

$$
f(x)=\cos^{3}{\left(x \right)}.
$$

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
f=u^{3},\qquad u=\cos{\left(x \right)}.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=3 u^{2},\qquad \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=- \sin{\left(x \right)}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\\&=(3 u^{2})\cdot(- \sin{\left(x \right)})\\&=- 3 \sin{\left(x \right)} \cos^{2}{\left(x \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Given that the velocity is $v(t)=2 \csc^{2}{\left(t \right)},$ the acceleration $a(t)$ of the particle is given by the derivative of the velocity with respect to time. Find the function $a(t).$

$a(t)=$
{{field-1}}$\cdot \operatorname{cot}t$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we write

$$
v(t)=2{csc}^{2}(t).
$$

Now, we see that $v(t)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
v=2{u}^{2},\,u=\operatorname{csc}t.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}u}=4u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=-\operatorname{csc}t\operatorname{cot}t.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & ={v}^{'}(t) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t} \\  & =4u\cdot (-\operatorname{csc}t\operatorname{cot}t) \\  & =(4\operatorname{csc}t)\cdot (-\operatorname{csc}t\operatorname{cot}t) \\  & =-4{csc}^{2}t\operatorname{cot}t.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express
$$
f(x) = -9(\sin{(x)})^{3}.
$$

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function
$$
f = -9u^{3}, \qquad u = \sin{(x)}.
$$

Differentiating, we get
$$
\dfrac{\textrm df}{\textrm d u} = -27u^2, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \cos{(x)}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get
\begin{align*}
f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt]

& = -27u^2 \cdot \cos{(x)}\\[5pt]

&=\bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-27\sin^2{(x)}\cos{(x)}}.
\end{align*}

Given that the velocity is $v(t)=8 \csc^{2}{\left(t \right)},$ the acceleration $a(t)$ of the particle is given by the derivative of the velocity with respect to time. Find the function $a(t).$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
$a(t)=$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
$\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡t$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we write

$$
v(t)=8{csc}^{2}⁡(t).
$$

Now, we see that $v(t)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
v=8{u}^{2},\,u=\operatorname{csc}⁡t.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}u}=16u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=-\operatorname{csc}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & ={v}^{′}(t) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t} \\  & =16u\cdot (-\operatorname{csc}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t) \\  & =(16\operatorname{csc}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{csc}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t) \\  & =-16{csc}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$
